Gurney suggested @akk{a-a i-qu!-la}, ‘may they not fall silent’, and this is generally accepted by recent translators; alternatively one might propose @akk{a-a i-BANDA₃-la} < @i{ay ibbaṭlā}, ‘may they not cease’. variants.reconstruction:
%n š[a nit]taqqû | mê | nād(āt)i
#note: See @bib{RN117@854}: “The spareness of the language means that the line is ambiguous. The passage is usually understood to refer to libations of water made to the Euphrates as a @i{numen loci} or on its bank. The Hittite paraphrase reports that Gilgameš and Enkidu made offerings to the sun god on the banks of the Euphrates but says nothing of where the water came from (@bib{RN314@108-9}). The present line must be connected with the repeated digging of wells during the journey to the Cedar Forest (SB IV 5 // 38 // 83 // 125 // 166). Accordingto the Yale tablet, some of the water so acquired had to be poured out in libation to Šamaš and Lugalbanda (OB III 268-71). It seems to me that the present line makes the point that the libations comprised water from the Euphrates itself. Travellers from Babylonia to Lebanon had to follow the Euphrates upstream for much of the way, and wells dug in its vicinity could easily be imagined to contain water from the river.”

#note: See @bib{RN117@862}: “This couplet follows the same pattern as SB I 99-100, where the mother goddess fashions Anu’s @i{zikru} (‘word, idea’) ‘in her heart’ (@i{ina libbīša}), with the result that Enkidu is created. While @i{na-a-ri} in l. 212 could be ‘singer’ rather than ‘river’, it does not seem likely that a minstrel has been singing, and all recent translators opt for ‘river’. The river is presumed to be the Ḫubur, the Babylonian Styx. What the ‘word/idea’ of this river might be is unknown. Instead I follow the suggestion of A. Cavigneaux that this line is related to the passage of the Death of Bilgames in which the Euphrates is diverted by damming while the hero’s tomb is built in its bed (@bib{RN24@11}). The spelling @akk{ZIK-ru} is thus for @i{sikru} or @i{sekēru}, so written because it was misunderstood under the influence of SB I 100.”
